facts.fact_text: On 12 February 1983, a number of Guadeloupe independence movements and trade unions held a public demonstration at Basse-Terre.
The applicant took part in the public demonstration at Basse-Terre on 12 February 1983.
The demonstration on 12 February 1983 was held by various independence movements in the Champ d'Arbaud, Basse-Terre, from 9 a.m. onwards.
The demonstration on 12 February 1983 took the form of a procession through the streets of Basse-Terre.
Demonstrators set off at 10.30 a.m. on 12 February 1983 and marched through the streets of Basse-Terre chanting slogans hostile to the police and the judiciary.
During the procession on 12 February 1983, graffiti were daubed in paint on various buildings, in particular the Institut d'émission d'Outre-mer, known as the 'Central Treasury'.
At ten past eleven on 12 February 1983, the demonstrators reached the Basse-Terre police station and assembled in front of it.

During the demonstration on 12 February 1983, there was a violent tirade against Police Officer Beaugendre, who was accused of betrayal, after which the crowd rhythmically chanted 'BEAUGENDRE-MAKO! UN JOU OU KE PAYE' (One day you will pay).
During the demonstration on 12 February 1983, the procession made a lengthy halt in front of the Law Courts in order to insult the judges.
During the demonstration on 12 February 1983, the procession made a lengthy halt outside the prison in order to demonstrate solidarity with the imprisoned militants.
The Principal Public Prosecutor's complaint of 1 June 1983 was brought under Article 113 of Decree no. 72-468 of 9 June 1972 regulating the profession of avocat.
At a disciplinary hearing held under Article 104 of Decree no. 72-468 of 9 June 1972, the Guadeloupe Bar Council adopted a decision on 25 July 1983.
On 12 December 1983, the Basse-Terre Court of Appeal reversed the Bar Council's decision of 25 July 1983.
On 12 December 1983, the Basse-Terre Court of Appeal imposed the disciplinary penalty of a reprimand on Mr Ezelin, a heavier penalty than a warning.
The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 sentenced Mr Ezelin to the disciplinary penalty of a reprimand and awarded costs against him.
On 19 June 1985, the Court of Cassation (First Civil Division) delivered a judgment dismissing the applicant's appeal on points of law.

Article 106 of Decree no. 72-468 of 9 June 1972 regulating the profession of avocat provides that any contravention of statutes or regulations, infringement of professional rules or breach of integrity, honour or discretion, even relating to non-professional matters, shall render the avocat responsible liable to the disciplinary sanctions listed in Article 107.

Article 107 of Decree no. 72-468 of 9 June 1972 regulating the profession of avocat provides that the disciplinary penalties shall be: a warning; a reprimand; suspension for a period not exceeding three years; striking off the roll of avocats or list of trainees or withdrawal of honorary status.
Avocats are bound by the oath they take when entering upon their duties.

Section 1 of the Act of 15 June 1982 on the procedure applicable in the event of professional misconduct by an avocat at a court hearing provides that the wording of the avocat's oath is: 'I swear, as an avocat, to defend and counsel in a dignified, conscientious, independent and humane manner.'

In a judgment of 9 June 1964, the Court of Cassation (First Civil Division) held that the avocat's oath also bound him in all circumstances not to deviate from the respect due to the courts and to the public authorities.

In a judgment of 30 June 1965 (Criminal Division, Bouvier), the Court of Cassation held that an avocat, while being entitled to protest at any infringement of the rights of the defence, must refrain from any expression which would reflect on the honour or discretion of a judge.

The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 found that during the demonstration on 12 February 1983, serious threats were continually made against a police constable and insults uttered against various other persons, including a judge of the Court of Appeal, a well-known regional figure and the judiciary as a whole.

The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 found that the walls of the Law Courts and of the département council building were covered with particularly offensive and insulting graffiti directed against the same persons during the demonstration on 12 February 1983.

The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 found that Mr Ezelin, who formed part of the procession notably when it halted in front of the police station, the Law Courts and the prison, could not have failed to see the insulting and offensive graffiti being painted in very large letters on all the walls of the Law Courts and of the council building, and could not have failed to hear the threats and insults directed against the same people.

Article 226, first paragraph of the French Criminal Code provides that anyone who by his acts or by means of the written or spoken word has publicly attempted to bring discredit on any action or decision taken by a court, in a manner likely to impair the authority or independence of the judiciary, shall be liable to imprisonment for not less than one month and not more than six months and a fine of not less than 500 francs and not more than 90,000 francs, or to only one of these two penalties.

The Chairman of the Guadeloupe Bar's letter of 14 March 1983 stated that Mr Ezelin had not been carrying a banner with another person but had been carrying a placard on his own bearing the words 'Trade Union of the Guadeloupe Bar against the Security and Freedom Act'.
The Chairman of the Guadeloupe Bar's letter of 14 March 1983 stated that no act, gesture or words insulting to the judiciary could be attributed to Mr Ezelin.
The Chairman of the Guadeloupe Bar's letter of 14 March 1983 stated that Mr Ezelin's participation in the demonstration had been confined to protesting at the use of the 'Security and Freedom' Act.

The Chairman of the Guadeloupe Bar concluded in his letter of 14 March 1983 that, even assuming the worst as regards Mr Ezelin, the Chief Superintendent's report did not accuse him of any insulting gesture, act or words.

The Chairman of the Guadeloupe Bar concluded in his letter of 14 March 1983 that Mr Ezelin could not have incurred any liability under Article 226 of the French Criminal Code in exercising his right to join a demonstration which had not been prohibited, carrying a placard with the words 'Trade Union of the Guadeloupe Bar against the Security and Freedom Act'.

The Bar Council's decision of 25 July 1983 found that Mr Ezelin's refusal to make a statement to the investigating judge was prompted by anxieties based on Article 105 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure and a concern to comply with Article 89 of Decree no. 72-468 of 9 June 1972, as some of the persons summoned by the investigating judge had previously consulted him as a lawyer.

The Bar Council's decision of 25 July 1983 found that Mr Ezelin, having been informed of the charge under Article 226 of the French Criminal Code, was justified in relying on the provisions of Article 105 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Bar Council's decision of 25 July 1983 found that Mr Ezelin's refusal to make a statement could not be regarded as contempt for justice and the judiciary.

The Bar Council's decision of 25 July 1983 noted that if Mr Ezelin's refusal had been deemed sufficiently serious to amount to obstructing the normal course of proceedings, the investigating judge would not have failed to avail himself of the provisions of Article 109 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure, nor the prosecution to make the appropriate applications before the discharge order was made.

The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 found that it was not alleged that Mr Ezelin took part in the demonstration any more actively than by his constant presence and by carrying a placard.

The Basse-Terre Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 December 1983 found that Mr Ezelin was at the demonstration in his capacity as an avocat, since he carried a placard announcing his profession, and at no time did he dissociate himself from the demonstrators' offensive and insulting acts or leave the procession.

The Court of Cassation's judgment of 19 June 1985 stated that the Basse-Terre Court of Appeal did not hold Mr Ezelin liable in virtue of a collective responsibility for criminal offences committed by other demonstrators.

The Court of Cassation's judgment of 19 June 1985 stated that the Basse-Terre Court of Appeal had found that Mr Ezelin, who was at the demonstration as an avocat and had heard the threats and insults and seen the offensive graffiti daubed on the walls of the Law Courts, did not at any time express his disapproval of these excesses or leave the procession in order to dissociate himself from these criminal acts.

The Court of Cassation's judgment of 19 June 1985 held that the Basse-Terre Court of Appeal was entitled to infer that Mr Ezelin, who had refused to give evidence without justifying his refusal on the basis of Article 105 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure or of professional confidentiality, had committed a breach of the law and of discretion vis-à-vis the investigating judge amounting to a disciplinary offence.
